summary: This topic moves children from reading coordinates to PRODUCING them: given a pair (x, y), plot the point; given a partly-drawn polygon, reason out and plot a missing vertex, then draw the sides. The key reasoning is that the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines shares one neighbour's x-value and another neighbour's y-value, so completion is derived from coordinates and shape properties rather than guessed by eye. The two dominant errors are reversal (plotting up-then-across) and completing 'by eye' from appearance instead of reasoning from the coordinates.
misconceptions: Reversal when plotting — going up before across, so the point lands in the mirror position (e.g. plots (5,4) at 4-across-5-up).
Completing a polygon by eye/appearance rather than reasoning from coordinates and shape properties, giving a wrong missing vertex.
Counting squares instead of numbered lines when plotting, producing off-by-one positions.
Joining vertices in the wrong order, producing a crossed or incorrect polygon even when the points are right.

activities.title: Plot-and-complete on a numbered grid
steps: Plot a given point by finding the x-line first, travelling up to the y-line, and marking the intersection, counting from the origin against the numbered lines.
Plot (5,4) and then (4,5) and compare: show they land in different places to make the along-then-up order explicit.

Given three vertices of a genuine square, e.g. (1,1), (1,4) and (4,4) (whose fourth vertex is (4,1), a 3-by-3 square with four equal sides), STATE the fourth coordinate aloud before plotting it, then plot it and draw the sides; check all four side lengths are equal and all four corners are right angles so the figure is genuinely a square.
Check the completed figure is the intended polygon: right angles and matching opposite sides for a rectangle, right angles and four equal sides for a square.

Repeat with three vertices of a rectangle, e.g. (1,1), (1,4), (5,4) whose fourth vertex is (5,1), giving a 4-by-3 rectangle, so the shared-x / shared-y reasoning transfers and children see that unequal sides (4 and 3) make a rectangle, not a square.
activities.insight: A point's location is fixed by reading x (across) then y (up) from the origin, and the missing vertex of a rectangle or square whose sides run along the grid lines can be reasoned out because it shares one neighbour's x and another neighbour's y; 'looks right' is replaced by 'is right' when the drawn sides form the named shape, with right angles at every corner and matching side lengths — four equal sides for a square, equal opposite sides for a rectangle.

activities.title: Which coordinate completes the shape? — diagnostic choices
steps: Choose which coordinate completes a given genuine square, e.g. three vertices (1,1),(1,4),(4,4) whose correct fourth vertex is (4,1), from options that include the reversed pair and a plausible but wrong by-eye value.
Explain WHY the chosen coordinate is correct in terms of shared x and shared y, not appearance.
Match a set of plotted points to their coordinate labels.
Plot a given set of points to form a rectangle and join them in order.
activities.insight: Identifying the correct missing vertex, and rejecting the reversal and by-eye distractors, shows that the vertex is determined by the coordinates and shape structure, not by how the figure looks.

activities.title: Reveal how a completed shape's coordinates relate
steps: On a completed rectangle with all vertices labelled, tap each corner to reveal how its coordinates relate to its neighbours (which x it shares, which y it shares).
Before a 'where must the fourth corner go?' answer is revealed, predict the coordinate and give a reason based on the shared values.
Trace the along-then-up path from the origin to each labelled vertex.
activities.insight: Even on a worked, labelled figure the child can see the structural pattern — each vertex shares an x with one neighbour and a y with another — which is the reasoning needed to complete a polygon.

checkQuestion: Show a grid with three vertices of a square marked and labelled: (1,1), (1,4) and (5,4). First (READ): 'Point to each marked vertex and tell me what its two numbers mean.' Then (PRODUCE): 'Plot the fourth vertex to complete the square, write its coordinates, and draw the sides.' Watch both the reading and the plotting.
checkAnswer: READ: each point is located across (x) then up (y) from the origin — e.g. (5,4) is 5 across, 4 up. PRODUCE: the fourth vertex is (5,1) — it shares the x-value (5) of (5,4) and the y-value (1) of (1,1); plotted at 5-across-1-up, completing the square with vertical and horizontal sides.
